speakeroldname: Mr. J. J. E. GUERIN (St. Ann):
subsubtopic: PROPOSED TARIFF INCREASE ON UNITED STATES PRODUCT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may seem rather anomalous for me representing one of the unban districts to take part in a debate which pertains almost exclusively to agriculturists. We have heard a great deal about protection, about the protection of agriculturists, 'but at the same time why should we not think a little of the protection of the consuming public whom we city members are elected to represent? I have not seen any slump in the price of eggs during many years. From my experience and from what I hear and read in the press the price of eggs throughout the winter season is always over the dollar mark per dozen, which I think is a very lucrative price for a common article of diet. I had no idea that the consumption of eggs amongst our people was as great as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) told us it was. Agriculturists might do a little better if they were to improve their grade of hens. Only recently, I had an opportunity of visiting the agricultural college at La Trappe and there I found hens called the Chanticleer, hens which laid practically every day, over 300 eggs in the year. The matter is simply one of cultivating the hen and bringing about a proper breed in order to have a more prolific crop of eggs.
What I rise particularly to dwell on is the question of public health in regard to eggs. We hear of eggs being imported from Australia and China. Anybody knows that such eggs are unfit for human consumption and if such eggs are imported, especially in bulk, it is nothing short of criminal to allow them to be put on the market for human consumption. When I was mayor of Montreal in 1911 I remember a consignment of Chinese eggs arriving in that city, which were examined and found to be practically putrid. The Board of Health endeavoured to stop their use and the importers sued the city fo.r interfering with their business. Naturally, in all things litigious the wheels of justice grind very slowly and these eggs were sequestrated for several months whilst the learned judge was coming to a conclusion as to whether they were fit for human use or not. Finally, after several months, he concluded that, for sufficient reasons, the city had no right to confiscate the eggs, and we at once proceeded to seize the eggs more effectively in order to have them destroyed at the public dump. But what was our amazement when we found that the eggs had been taken away in some manner that I do not understand, through some of the intricacies of the law, and had been sold to confectioners and others, so that we felt that we had eaten all those eggs.

If there is anything that we should do more than another it is absolutely to prohibit the importation of eggs in bulk. There is no more prolific medium for the development of micro-organisms than the albumen of eggs, and we know perfectly well that when, in these oriental countries, eggs are broken into cans which are sealed up and sent thousands of miles away for the consumption of white people, the same precaution or trouble is not taken as if the orientals were going to eat the eggs themselves. One rotten egg in a barrel of eggs is sufficient to make the whole barrelful rotten inside of- a week or two.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED TARIFF INCREASE ON UNITED STATES PRODUCT
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman
remember that the statement was made on the floor of this House, I think in January, that there were seventeen carloads of Chinese eggs in storage in Montreal?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED TARIFF INCREASE ON UNITED STATES PRODUCT
speechtext:
I was not present at the
time. It may have been said. I hope, however, they will be used for manure purposes to increase the fecundity of the ground in order that we may grow more grain to feed the hens that will lay fresh eggs. I would not advise the use for human consumption of the eggs to which the hon. gentleman refers. There is no doubt that in dealing with the question of contamination we cannot be too careful in regard to eggs, especially those imported from another country. These eggs come to us in bulk, bringing with them probably some germs of disease of which we know nothing and which we never suspect, so that we run the risk of infecting all our people. We remember that during the year 1917 we had a visitation of a disease which we called Spanish influenza or grippe. It was not grippe at all, nor was it influenza in the ordinary acceptation of that word. It was some imported disease which I firmly believe came from the Orient; it bore all the earmarks of the bubonic plague. Where did it come from? We know that mingling with our soldiers there were Chinese, Japanese and other orientals who might have carried the germs of the disease with them. I ask, therefore, is there anything more menacing than the importation of these oriental eggs in bulk? To me it is unspeakable; it is something that should not be tolerated. Not only should there be a high duty on eggs coming in bulk, but they should be absolutely prohibited.
Now, I am in favour of protection-protection for the people of my constituency. I want to protect them against the high cost of living, so that they may be able to buy reasonably eggs, of which they use large

Imports oj Eggs
quantities. I want to protect the fathers of families of ten and fifteen children, such as we have in Montreal and in the province of Quebec generally. It is imperative that these children be given wholesome food. We should therefore put every facility in the way of their fathers to get eggs, among other things, at a reasonable price. An increase of five or eight cents a dozen on eggs would make them prohibitive to the father of a large family, and I am not in favour of that.
In the debate this afternoon some hon. gentlemen seemed to favour a tariff as a means of retaliation, while others to whom I have listened want a tariff for the purpose of protecting the farmer. I am quite sympathetic with the farmer but I am more sympathetic with the public in general. In any case I do not believe in legislating for the sake of retaliation; I do not think any good comes of such legislation. Whatever laws we pass we should enact with a view to benefiting our people in some way or other, and I do not see what benefit can accrue from legislation that is framed merely for the purpose of hitting back; nor do I believe in legislation which will result in misery to the greater number of our people. For these reasons I purpose voting against the proposition. I feel that the interests of the majority should be safeguarded and I believe that a proper system of inspection and an absolute prohibition of eggs in bulk would be a step in the right direction.

speechtext:
This is an interesting resolution, the discussion of which may prove of value to the House and perhaps to the country as well. It seems to me that before parliament is asked to pass a resolution having for its object the remedying of a certain condition of affairs, we should have some evidence as to the cause of that condition. Very little has been said to-day about the causes of the alleged condition of the egg-producing industry in Canada. The hon. member who proposes the resolution (A{r. Esling) comes from British Columbia, and another hon. member who has spoken in favour of it also represents a constituency in that part of the country. I am led to believe that the poultry industry ol British Columbia is an important one which is suffering from disabilities with which the people in other parts of Canada are perhaps not familiar. We find therefore, from time tc time, that many resolutions are introduced in this House and discussed by members from British Columbia who are interested in the production and marketing of eggs. To me it seems but reasonable that before any action
is taken, such as is proposed in this resolution, we should inquire of these members the reasons why, from a province like British Columbia where the climatic conditions are favourable and where many other conditions conduce to the successful raising of poultry, such as cheap material for buildings, the complaint comes most often that something must be done to remedy the evils existing in the egg market.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has anticipated a question I was about to put as to the high cost of production. He says that it is due to the high price of wheat, by which I presume he means the high price of feed generally. In my opinion, if the basic conditions in this industry are as they have been stated to be, and if care is exercised in the production and sale of eggs, the results should be reasonably satisfactory. If the various conditions surrounding the poultry business are as they ought to be, including climate, distribution, and so forth, I see no reason why the industry should not succeed.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni touched briefly in his remarks on the cost of feed. He said that certain reductions had been made in the freight rate on grain going through British Columbia for export, and he contended that reductions should be conceded in the freight on grain going into that province for home consumption. When the hon. member made the first remark, to the effect that the remedy would be found in part tc consist in a reduction in the rates on wheat, I applauded for the reason that I felt the statement was in line with something that should have been done many years ago. I observed that some of my Conservative friends across the way smiled when they heard me applauding, as though they thought, " Here is another of those representatives from tht west insisting on a reduction in the freight rate on the things they want to sell." Now, that was not the idea I had in mind at all. I was merely thinking that a reasonable and fair rate should be fixed, for the benefit of Canadian* living in British Columbia, on the grain they have to buy in order to keep one of their industries going. There should be given to them a freight rate just as fair and reasonable as that which applies to the wheat or other grain produced on the western prairie or elsewhere in Canada and consumed by the people of China, Japan or Europe. That should be adopted as a fair and reasonable principle, provided it costs no more for the railroad to
Imports of Eggs

bring to Vancouver a carload of grain destined to be fed to poultry in British Columbia, than it does to haul a carload of grain bound for the Orient or other world markets. Given that condition, I see no good reason why grain should not be moved at the same rate. It may be that the railroad officials could defend the existing rates. I am perfectly satisfied they could; but on the basis of fairness and common sense I see no good reason why those rates should not be adjusted.
The hon. member for St. Ann (Mr. Guerin) mentioned another condition that is absolutely necessary in connection with the raising of poultry or any other kind of stock, namely, that the right strains of poultry only be kept and brought up to their highest efficiency. Given these basic conditions-that is to say, the use of the best egg-producing strains of fowls, fed at the lowest prices which world market conditions permit; the favourable climatic and other conditions that are characteristic of Bi'itish Columbia, and the concession of reasonable distributing and marketing facilities-there is no reason in the world why British Columbia should not produce and market eggs in competition with any other part of the continent. In considering the necessary facilities I have reference not only to climatic conditions but also to cheap material fci the erection of buildings, the long season out-of-doors, and cheap electric light in the poultry houses to extend the period of laying.
Some hon. members referred to eggs produced in Florida, Georgia, and other southern states. I do not think poultrymen in British Columbia or elsewhere in Canada need fear the competition of the hen in the southern states. The great bulk of the soil of Florida, and I believe the same is true of Georgia, is impregnated with pure sand, and there has to be considerable outlay in enriching that soil before it can be made to yield the green stuffs or other foods necessary for the production of eggs. Then the cost of transportation to the northern market has to be borne in mind. Furthermore there is the disability under which the hen lives in hot weather. I am satisfied that any poultry producer in the House would probably admit it is harder to overcome the handicap of hot weather in the case of poultry than it is to overcome the disability which results from cold weather Providence seems tc have provided the chicken with feathers suitable for defence against a cold climate, but I do not know of any provision of nature which gives it relief in a hot climate.

speechtext: Why not provide the hen with rubber boots and snow-shoes?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED TARIFF INCREASE ON UNITED STATES PRODUCT
speechtext:
Sometimes we equip the sled dogs in northern latitudes with moccasins but we have not yet reached the stage where we make such provisions for hens.
Taking the facts which I have enumerated into consideration-climatic conditions, the cost of feed, and the cost of transportation- I think it would be well for hon. members to rid their minds of the impression that competition from the southern states by reason of milder weather in the winter and hotter weather at other times of the year is going to run the Canadian hen off the market. There is of course the further fact that the time consumed in bringing the southern eggs to the northern market would make them far from "strictly fresh" eggs when they landed here. I am firmly convinced that if feed of all kinds can be provided for the British Columbia poultry raiser at reasonable prices, through a fairer freight rate, it will be of great assistance to him. In the winter he is able to raise green stuffs and to feed his poultry out-of-doors. He has that advantage over the producer on the prairie or in the east, ll also think that if the poultry producers of that province adopted the principle of co-operative marketing they would find it a decided advantage.
Before passing on to another phase of the question I should like to express my appreciation of the suggestion made by the hon. member for St. Ann in that no eggs in bulk that are unfit for human consumption should be allowed into this country for that purpose. If such importations are bad for the people of this country they should1 be absolutely excluded; there should be no tinkering with the matter. On the other hand, if eggs in bulk are good for our people they should be allowed in as freely as possible consistent with justice. It is possible that such eggs may be needed as raw material in certain lines of industry, in which case I would allow their admission provided their use is confined entirely to the object intended.

Not a particle. But the members who thundered it and lauded it to the skies now come into this House and vote for the government that will not take one step in that direction.
The budget is coming this session, and I ask hon. members to be very careful; they do not know what they are going to be called on to vote for in that budget. This government is capable of anything in the way of a convolution-anything at all-and they will have to support it. This government, if it felt it could sustain its position another hour by putting the duty on eggs up to eight cents a dozen, would do it and never turn a hair, and hon. gentlemen would come up and vote for it; they would have to. Not a particle. Hon.
gentlemen have been quoting that speech for ten years, and the quotation is usually the best part of the speeches they have delivered. That speech was a confirmation from beginning to end of the protective principle and its application, but the protective principle does not mean that every time you touch the tariff you must raise it. No, see that it is left conformable to the protective principle, but it must still mean protection for industry in this country. We must submit to one of two alternatives: a Canadian wage scale as low as that of any other country where the competing article is produced, either that or the protective system. Those who choose the first, let them consistently follow it through, but those who choose the second, let them follow it through with equal consistency and apply it to all classes of Canadian production.

The protective system
is one that, to the utmost that it can be done, applies the protective principle to every branch of industry in the country. It cannot be done with equal application to all; that cannot be done in any cotmtry in the world. The bigger the volume of export compared to home consumption, the less can it be applied, but to every industry it can be applied to a degree, and to all vital industries it can be applied with beneficial results. But the system must be adopted, no matter whether it falls unevenly in its benefits or not, or you must submit to the condition of a wage scale in this country as low as that of any other country where the competing article is produced.
